name: Hosea

overview.author: Hosea son of Beeri, a prophet to the northern kingdom (1:1).
overview.date: About 755–715 BC, during the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel and Uzziah through Hezekiah of Judah.
overview.audience: The northern kingdom of Israel (often called Ephraim) in its last prosperous and then chaotic decades before Assyria destroyed Samaria in 722 BC.
overview.setting: Israel enjoyed wealth under Jeroboam II but fell into Baal worship, political intrigue, and rapid turnover of kings.
overview.purpose: To expose Israel’s spiritual adultery, announce judgment, and display God’s steadfast, covenant love that will heal and restore His people.
overview.structure: Hosea’s marriage to Gomer as a living parable (1–3), followed by oracles of Israel’s sin and judgment interwoven with God’s love (4–14).

items.title: How can I give you up?

themes.title: Spiritual Adultery
themes.text: Israel’s idolatry is pictured as a wife’s unfaithfulness to her husband.

themes.title: Steadfast Love (Hesed)
themes.text: God’s covenant love persists despite Israel’s betrayal.

themes.title: Knowledge of God
themes.text: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (4:6). God desires steadfast love and knowledge of Him more than sacrifices (6:6).

themes.title: Judgment and Discipline
themes.text: Israel will reap the whirlwind of its sin, going into exile.

themes.title: Redemption
themes.text: Like Hosea buying back Gomer, God will redeem His people.

themes.title: Return and Healing
themes.text: God calls Israel to return and promises, “I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely” (14:4).

christInBook.text: “Out of Egypt I called my son” is fulfilled in Jesus’ return from Egypt (Matthew 2:15).
Hosea redeeming Gomer pictures Christ redeeming His bride at great cost (Ephesians 5:25).
Jesus quotes this verse twice to rebuke the Pharisees (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).
“Not my people” becoming “my people” is applied to Gentiles in Christ (Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10).
Victory over death and Sheol is quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:55.

crossReferences.note: The history of Israel in Hosea’s time.
Paul quotes Hosea for Gentile inclusion.
Faithless Israel as an unfaithful wife.

reflection: How does Hosea’s marriage help you understand God’s love for you?
What “lovers” compete for your heart’s loyalty to God?
Hosea 6:6 says God wants steadfast love and knowledge of Him. How can you grow in knowing Him?
Where have you sown wind and reaped whirlwind (8:7)?
What would returning to the Lord with words (14:2) look like for you today?

chapterList.title: Hosea’s Wife and Children
chapterList.summary: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, “a wife of whoredom,” as a picture of Israel’s unfaithfulness. Their children receive symbolic names: Jezreel (judgment), No Mercy, and Not My People. Yet God promises that one day they will be called “Children of the living God.”
questions: Why would God ask Hosea to enter such a painful marriage?
What do the children’s names communicate?
How does 1:10 turn judgment into hope?

chapterList.title: I Will Allure Her
chapterList.summary: Israel credited Baal for grain, wine, and oil that God gave. God will strip her and block her path. But then He will “allure her” into the wilderness, speak tenderly, and betroth her forever in righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy, and faithfulness.
questions: Who did Israel credit for her blessings (2:8)?
Why does God lead her into the wilderness (2:14)?
What qualities mark God’s betrothal (2:19–20)?

chapterList.title: Hosea Redeems Gomer
chapterList.summary: God tells Hosea to love his wife again, though she loves another. Hosea buys her back for silver and barley and asks her to be faithful. So Israel will be without king or sacrifice for a time, then return to seek the LORD and David their king.
questions: What did it cost Hosea to redeem Gomer?
How does this picture Christ’s redemption?
Who is “David their king” in 3:5?

chapterList.title: No Knowledge of God
chapterList.summary: God brings a charge: there is no faithfulness, steadfast love, or knowledge of God in the land. “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.” Priests have failed to teach; people consult wooden idols and engage in cultic prostitution.
questions: What three things are missing in the land (4:1)?
Why are priests blamed (4:6–9)?
How does a “spirit of whoredom” lead people astray (4:12)?

chapterList.title: Judgment on Priests and Kings
chapterList.summary: Priests, people, and king are judged. Ephraim and Judah turn to Assyria for help, but God will be like a lion to them. He will return to His place “until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face.”
questions: Why was turning to Assyria a sin?
How is God like a moth and like a lion (5:12–14)?
What does God wait for (5:15)?

chapterList.title: Let Us Press On to Know the LORD
chapterList.summary: The people say, “Come, let us return... he has torn us, that he may heal us... let us press on to know the LORD.” But their love is like a morning cloud. God says, “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice.”
questions: What sounds good about 6:1–3?
Why is their love compared to dew (6:4)?
How does Jesus apply 6:6 (Matthew 9:13)?

chapterList.title: Like a Heated Oven
chapterList.summary: Israel’s leaders burn with intrigue like an oven, and kings fall. Ephraim is “a cake not turned,” and “like a dove, silly and without sense,” calling to Egypt and Assyria. They do not cry to God from the heart.
questions: What does a “cake not turned” mean (7:8)?
Why is Ephraim like a silly dove (7:11)?
What does it mean to cry to God from the heart (7:14)?

chapterList.title: Sowing the Wind
chapterList.summary: Israel made kings and idols without God. “They sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.” God wrote His laws, but they regarded them as strange. Israel has forgotten its Maker.
questions: What does sowing wind and reaping whirlwind mean?
How did Israel make kings without God (8:4)?
How can we forget our Maker while staying busy?

chapterList.title: Days of Punishment
chapterList.summary: Israel will not remain in the land but return to “Egypt” and eat unclean food in Assyria. The prophet is considered a fool. Ephraim will be fruitless and become wanderers among the nations.
questions: Why does joy disappear in exile (9:1–5)?
How did people treat the prophet (9:7–8)?
What does it mean that they will be “wanderers among the nations” (9:17)?

chapterList.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
chapterList.summary: Israel was a luxuriant vine, but the more fruit it had, the more altars it built. Its calf idol will be carried to Assyria. “Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD.”
questions: How did prosperity lead to more idolatry (10:1)?
What does God call them to sow (10:12)?
Where might your heart need its fallow ground broken up?

chapterList.title: How Can I Give You Up?
chapterList.summary: God remembers loving Israel as a child: “Out of Egypt I called my son.” He taught Ephraim to walk and led them with cords of kindness. Though they turned away, God says, “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?... My heart recoils within me.”
questions: How does God describe His fatherly love (11:1–4)?
How is 11:1 fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:15)?
What does 11:8–9 reveal about God’s heart?

chapterList.title: Jacob’s Story
chapterList.summary: Ephraim feeds on wind and multiplies lies. God recalls Jacob, who strove with God and wept and sought His favor. “So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God.”
questions: Why remember Jacob’s story (12:3–4)?
What does God call them to in 12:6?
How does wealth deceive Ephraim (12:8)?

chapterList.title: O Death, Where Are Your Plagues?
chapterList.summary: Ephraim once exalted, but sinned with Baal and made idols. God fed them in the wilderness, but when they were full, they forgot Him. Yet God says, “Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol?... O Death, where are your plagues?”
questions: How did fullness lead to forgetting God (13:6)?
What does it mean that God is the only Savior (13:4)?
How does Paul use 13:14 in 1 Corinthians 15:55?

chapterList.title: Return and Be Healed
chapterList.summary: “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God.” Take words and say, “Take away all iniquity.” God promises, “I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely.” Israel will blossom like the lily. “The ways of the LORD are right.”
questions: What words does God give for repentance (14:2–3)?
What does God promise in 14:4–7?
How does 14:9 conclude the book?

tagline: The prophet’s marriage and God’s relentless love for an unfaithful people
readingPlan: 14 chapters: one chapter a day takes 14 days; two a day takes about 7 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
